claims.text: The initial material is an equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr random solid solution.
The random solid solution has high configurational entropy.
The random HfNbTaTiZr state has significant local lattice distortion.
The random state strongly scatters phonons across the entire frequency spectrum.
Thermal annealing or Monte Carlo treatment can induce chemical short-range order in HfNbTaTiZr.
Short-range ordering produces B2-like HfTi and TiZr binary clusters.
The B2-like binary clusters can form a percolating network.
Processing between 0.5 and 0.8 times the melting temperature permits SRO formation without full phase separation.
The percolating ordered-cluster network locally relaxes the lattice strain field.
The proposed strain relaxation results from atomic-radius matching within HfTi and TiZr pairs.
Transition from the random state to B2-like order reduces the local variance in atomic-size mismatch.
Reduced local lattice distortion decreases the scattering cross-section for high-frequency phonons.
Percolation of low-distortion regions creates continuous pathways for high-frequency phonon transport.
High-frequency phonons have longer mean free paths in the percolated ordered state.
Transport through the ordered pathways can outweigh scattering from the remaining random matrix and cluster boundaries.
Percolating B2-like order causes a net increase in lattice thermal conductivity relative to the random alloy.
Phonons above 5 THz exhibit increased group velocity in the ordered state.
Phonons above 5 THz exhibit increased lifetime in the ordered state.
Below the ordered-cluster percolation threshold, the system behaves like a random alloy and remains in the reduced-conductivity regime.
Macroscopic phase separation or large coherent precipitates restore the conductivity-decrease trend by introducing substantial interface scattering.

contradictions.description: The boundary predicts that an ordered but sub-percolation sample can remain in the reduced-conductivity regime, whereas the falsification rule treats lower conductivity in any ordered sample as falsifying regardless of its degree of percolation. A nonpercolated ordered sample could therefore simultaneously satisfy the proposed boundary and trigger falsification.
